About Our Team

We are a group of passionate students from FAST-NUCES, Lahore, driven by curiosity, innovation, and a desire to solve real-world problems through technology. We are particularly interested in software development, artificial intelligence, robotics, data science, and automation.

As computer science students, we enjoy exploring challenging ideas, learning new technologies, and turning creative concepts into practical solutions.
summary: EMBER is an interactive historical burning-activity explorer that turns decades of NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS active-fire observations into a responsible, place-based story. Its immersive globe, regional explorer, seasonal calendar, cross-sensor diagnostics, and printable Fire Season Passport help people investigate when and where satellites detected thermal anomalies without presenting detections as unique fires, burned area, causes, or observation coverage. EMBER keeps MODIS and VIIRS histories separate because their instruments and confidence semantics are not directly comparable. Every view exposes provenance, UTC dates, snapshot timing, provisional-record labels, and meaningful empty or failure states. The result makes a complex Earth-observation record accessible to students, researchers, planners, and curious communities while preserving the scientific limits needed for honest interpretation.
details:
EMBER is a deployable web atlas for exploring historical satellite-detected burning activity. The homepage uses a cinematic, scene-by-scene globe narrative; one mouse-wheel gesture advances one complete scene so the evidence graphic and its explanation are visible together. The regional explorer combines a MapLibre basemap with deck.gl aggregation and point inspection. The calendar shows named sensor histories by UTC day and compares a selected day only with prior same-month positive-detection days. The comparison view presents MODIS and VIIRS in independent panels and scales, while the printable Fire Season Passport turns a selected region, year, stream, and date into a one-page evidence sheet. A methodology route makes provenance, validation outcomes, and non-claims explicit.

EMBER uses a checked-in, reproducible NASA FIRMS snapshot derived from the Portolan FIRMS mirror, with raw observations classified by sensor, satellite, quality, time, and provenance. Positive detections are never treated as proof that unobserved areas were fire-free. Raw counts are not silently harmonized across sensors. An experimental cross-sensor calibration was evaluated with leakage-safe held-out years against an explicit baseline; because the release gates were not met, the public interface continues to show independent sensor histories instead of an invented combined truth.

The application was built with TypeScript, React, Next.js, Three.js/react-globe.gl, MapLibre GL, deck.gl, GSAP, and Playwright. It includes responsive desktop and mobile layouts, keyboard navigation, reduced-motion behavior, a non-WebGL fallback, explicit source-down and zero-row states, print styling, and automated unit, type, build, and end-to-end checks. The visual system is an original dark editorial treatment designed to make dense evidence legible without resembling a generic dashboard.

The intended impact is better public access to the long thermal-anomaly record and more careful conversations about fire activity. EMBER helps users discover seasonal patterns and inspect source rows while repeatedly distinguishing detected pixels from unique fires, burned area, cause, severity, risk, forecast skill, and observation coverage.
